strengths: Resolves significant open problems from COLT '25 by proving W[1]-hardness, which is stronger than previously known NP-hardness results for network verification and zonotope containment

Novel and non-trivial parameterized reduction from MULTICOLORED CLIQUE with linear dimension scaling—most hardness reductions allow unconstrained parameter growth, making the dimension constraint here a genuine technical contribution
Comprehensive treatment covering multiple related problems (positivity, surjectivity, maximum approximation, Lipschitz constants for multiple p values) with consistent hardness proofs
Provides tight ETH-based lower bounds of n^Ω(d) · poly(N) showing that simple enumeration algorithms are essentially optimal—a rare and valuable characterization
Clever technical contributions including homogenization technique for bias-free networks and well-motivated use of Sidon sets for ensuring label uniqueness
Includes both hardness and positive results: polynomial-time algorithm for L1 and FPT algorithm for L∞ on input convex neural networks
Well-written with clear exposition, helpful proof sketches in main text, detailed proofs in appendix, and illustrative figures
Extends hardness results beyond neural networks to zonotope problems in computational geometry and control theory, broadening impact
weaknesses: Limited practical relevance: adversarial hardness constructions with engineered spike and penalty functions do not represent realistic neural networks trained via gradient descent on real data
Narrow applicability: hardness constructions are specifically engineered problem instances without clear connection to properties of networks arising in practice

Incomplete treatment of approximation: open question remains for Lp-maximization with p ∈ (1, ∞); randomized approximation algorithm (Theorem 7.2) has worse running time than enumeration for practical d values
Restrictive tractable classes: positive results only apply to input convex neural networks (ICNNs), limiting insights into broader tractability conditions

Missing practical guidance: paper acknowledges difficulty in formulating general strategies to circumvent hardness in practice but does not deeply explore when hardness applies or how to identify tractable instances in real settings

No empirical or experimental validation: despite addressing practical problems like network verification, paper lacks investigation of hardness constructions' behavior or comparison with existing verification tools
Limited exploration of average-case or smoothed complexity: results are purely worst-case and do not address complexity on typical problem instances

Reduction technique is relatively standard: while dimension scaling is novel, the overall reduction strategy from MULTICOLORED CLIQUE becomes straightforward once the main technical challenge is identified

strengths: Resolves open problems from COLT '25 on parameterized complexity of neural network verification
Technically sophisticated reductions from Multicolored Clique and SAT problems with novel use of Sidon sets and carefully designed gadgets
Comprehensive coverage: establishes hardness for multiple problems (positivity, surjectivity, Lipschitz constant, zonotope containment, injectivity) and parameters (d and ℓ)
Matching upper and lower bounds: combines algorithmic upper bounds showing inclusion in XP with ETH-based lower bounds proving enumeration is near-optimal
Interesting conceptual contribution establishing connections between W-hierarchy and bounded-depth ReLU networks
Elegant homogenization technique (Definition 5.1, Lemma 5.2) for handling biases while proving hardness
Includes positive results: polynomial-time algorithm for L₁/L∞ Lipschitz constants on ICNNs; randomized FPT-approximation via subspace embeddings
Well-organized presentation with effective use of summary tables and illustrative figures
weaknesses: Limited practical implications: results confirm that enumeration is hard without suggesting what practitioners should do instead; significant gap between worst-case theory and practical verification approaches remains unaddressed
Incomplete complexity characterization: 2-layer ReLU Positivity shown to be in W[P] but not proven W[2]-hard; unclear whether ℓ-layer positivity is W[ℓ-1]-complete rather than just hard
Incremental extension from base case: once 2-layer W[1]-hardness is established, extensions to deeper networks follow somewhat mechanically, reducing novelty of results for ℓ≥3
Non-standard assumptions in Lipschitz constant results: requires oracle access for norm comparisons; weaker results for unbounded depth (para-NP rather than W[t]-hardness)
Complex and dense constructions: the W[ℓ]-hardness proofs (especially Theorem 5.4 Cases I-II) are intricate, making high-level insights difficult to extract even for experts
Limited guidance on avoiding hardness: acknowledgment that network structure matters (ICNNs, sparse weights) but minimal systematic study of when and how to exploit structure in practice
Zonotope containment results are largely consequence of existing duality with 2-layer ReLU positivity (Froese et al. 2025b) rather than independent contribution
Straightforward upper bounds: Section 3 provides standard enumeration algorithms without surprising algorithmic insights

strengths: Resolves open problems from Froese et al. (COLT '25) on parameterized complexity of neural network verification
Comprehensive and systematic treatment of multiple related problems (positivity, surjectivity, Lipschitz constants, zonotope containment) with hardness results for both parameters d and ℓ
Establishes matching upper and lower bounds, showing that naive enumeration algorithms running in n^((ℓ-1)d)·poly(N) are essentially optimal under ETH
Reveals interesting structural connection between network depth and the W-hierarchy, with W[ℓ-1]-hardness for (ℓ+1)-layer networks

Technical innovation in reductions: clever use of Sidon sets in Multicolored Clique reduction, novel homogenization technique for removing biases, and sophisticated Boolean formula simulation via ReLU networks
Balanced presentation including tractable special cases (input convex networks) and randomized approximation algorithms alongside hardness results
Well-structured paper with clear motivation, comprehensive preliminaries, and detailed proofs
weaknesses: Incomplete theoretical characterization: for ℓ ≥ 3 layers, it remains unknown whether positivity is contained in W[P], creating a gap in the theoretical picture

Homogenization technique (Definition 5.1) is somewhat opaque—the intuition for using y in the first layer and |y| in subsequent layers lacks clear motivation, and the interaction with bias cancellation deserves more explanation

Reduction from Weighted (Anti)Monotone t-Normalized SAT (Theorem 5.4) is highly complex, spanning multiple pages with intricate constructions of pc, sr,l, δD, γC functions; presentation could be more streamlined to improve verifiability
Limited practical applicability—hardness results don't suggest viable verification algorithms, and guidance for practitioners on handling these intractable problems is minimal
Paper length (31 pages) with dense presentation; some sections have repetitive constructions (Cases I and II in Theorem 5.4) that could be condensed

Limited discussion of approximation algorithms—while Section 8 on randomized FPT-approximation is interesting, the question of whether approximation is easier than exact computation deserves more thorough treatment
Para-NP-hardness results (Section 9, d=1 with unbounded ℓ) introduce additional complexity via base-n representations; relationship to main results could be clearer
No experimental validation despite explicit network constructions; examples of hard instances' size relative to practical networks would strengthen practical relevance
